items.title: How Burger King’s New Whopper Is Winning Back Customers | WSJ
items.author: The Wall Street Journal
items.content:
<article>Burger King is trying to convince America it has the best burger out—and that it’s worth paying for. The No. 2 U.S. burger chain by sales has charged its corporate chef with upgrading the sauces, buns and packaging for its food. Executives believe the improvements are helping it to stand out in the competitive fast-food market that often relies on discounts to bring in customers. But they are also having to convince restaurant operators that the changes are worth the investment even at a time when food costs are rising.

WSJ goes inside Burger King’s test kitchen at the company’s Miami headquarters and speaks with executives about how they’re seeking to gain more sales through juicier chicken nuggets and hotter Whoppers.

items.title: Why These $500 Japanese Jeans Have a Cult Following | WSJ Coveted
items.author: The Wall Street Journal
items.content:
<article>If you know good jeans, you know about Japanese denim. Perhaps no brand has garnered as fierce a following as Iron Heart. The so-called “Iron Heart Army” gathers on a clunky old Internet forum, discussing cotton origins, dip-dye varieties, shuttle looms, raw denim fading competitions and the mundanity of daily life. 

WSJ explores how a 69-year-old Japanese biker built the coveted denim brand.

items.title: Why 10K People Are Waiting to Search the Thames | WSJ
items.author: The Wall Street Journal
items.content:
<article>Once a desperate 18th-century fight for survival, mudlarking has evolved into one of London’s most coveted viral pastimes. The craft of scavenging the River Thames for lost relics at low tide has surged in popularity, leaving more than 10,000 hopeful treasure hunters stuck on a permit waitlist. 

WSJ joined mudlarks to learn how citizen archaeologists are unearthing London’s lost history in the mud.
